Main.sentence: Constitutional law is a body of law which defines the role, powers, and structure of different entities within a ___E:state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_(polity))___ , namely, the ___E:executive U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_(government))___ , the ___E:parliament U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament)___ or ___E:legislature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislature)___ , and the ___E:judiciary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judiciary)___ ; as well as the basic rights of citizens and their relationship with their governments, and in federal countries such as the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_States_Constitution)___ and ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada)___ , the relationship between the central government and state, provincial, or territorial governments.

Not all ___E:nation states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nation_state)___ have codified ___E:constitutions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution)___ , though all such states have a jus commune , or law of the land, that may consist of a variety of imperative and consensual rules.

These may include ___E:customary law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custom_(law))___ , ___E:conventions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_(norm))___ , ___E:statutory law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statutory_law)___ , ___E:judge-made law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precedent)___ , or ___E:international law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_law)___ .
Constitutional law deals with the fundamental principles by which the government exercises its authority.
In some instances, these principles grant specific powers to the government, such as the power to tax and spend for the welfare of the population.
Other times, constitutional principles act to place limits on what the government can do, such as prohibiting the arrest of an individual without sufficient cause.

In most nations, such as the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_constitutional_law)___ , ___E:India U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_India)___ , and ___E:Singapore U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Singapore)___ , constitutional law is based on the text of a document ratified at the time the nation came into being.

Other constitutions, notably ___E:that of the United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_Kingdom)___ ,   rely heavily on uncodified rules, as several legislative statutes and ___E:constitutional conventions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_convention_(political_custom))___ , their status within constitutional law varies, and the terms of conventions are in some cases strongly contested.
Constitutional laws can be considered second order rule making [clarification needed] or rules about making rules to exercise power.
It governs the relationships between the judiciary, the legislature and the executive with the bodies under its authority.
One of the key tasks of constitutions within this context is to indicate hierarchies and relationships of power.

For example, in a ___E:unitary state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_state)___ , the constitution will vest ultimate authority in one central administration and ___E:legislature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislature)___ , and ___E:judiciary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judiciary)___ , though there is often a delegation of power or authority to local or municipal authorities.

When a constitution establishes a ___E:federal state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_state)___ for instance as seen in India, it will identify multiple levels of government coexisting with exclusive or shared areas of jurisdiction over lawmaking, application and enforcement.

Some federal states, most notably the United States, have separate and parallel federal and state judiciaries, with each having its own hierarchy of courts with a supreme court for each state. ___E:India U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_system_of_India)___ , on the other hand, has one judiciary divided into district courts, high courts, and the ___E:Supreme Court of India U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_India)___ .
Human rights or ___E:civil liberties U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_liberties)___ form a crucial part of a country's constitution and uphold the rights of the individual against the state.

Most jurisdictions, like the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ and ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France)___ , have a codified constitution, with a ___E:bill of rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_of_rights)___ . ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada)___ is an example where the constitution is not codified, but includes the ___E:Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Charter_of_Rights_and_Freedoms)___ to protect human rights for Canadian citizens and residents.

Some countries like the ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom)___ have no entrenched document setting out fundamental rights; in those jurisdictions the constitution is composed of ___E:statute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute)___ , ___E:case law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_law)___ and ___E:convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_convention_(political_custom))___ .

A case named Entick v. Carrington  is a constitutional principle deriving from the common law. ___E:John Entick U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Entick)___ 's house was searched and ransacked by Sheriff Carrington.

Carrington argued that a warrant from a Government minister, the ___E:Earl of Halifax U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Montagu-Dunk,_2nd_Earl_of_Halifax)___ was valid authority, even though there was no statutory provision or court order for it. The court, led by ___E:Lord Camden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Pratt,_1st_Earl_Camden)___ stated that,
"The great end, for which men entered into society, was to secure their property.
That right is preserved sacred and incommunicable in all instances, where it has not been taken away or abridged by some public law for the good of the whole.
By the laws of England, every invasion of private property, be it ever so minute, is a trespass...
If no excuse can be found or produced, the silence of the books is an authority against the defendant, and the plaintiff must have judgment."

The ___E:common law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_law)___ and the ___E:civil law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_(legal_system))___ jurisdictions do not share the same constitutional law underpinnings. ___E:Common law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_law)___ nations, such as those in the Commonwealth as well as the United States, derive their legal systems from that of the United Kingdom, and as such place emphasis on judicial precedent,    whereby consequential court rulings (especially those by higher courts) are a ___E:source of law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stare_decesis)___ .

Civil law jurisdictions, on the other hand, place less emphasis on judicial review and only the parliament or legislature has the power to effect law. As a result, the structure of the judiciary differs significantly between the two, with common law judiciaries being ___E:adversarial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_system)___ and civil law judiciaries being ___E:inquisitorial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inquisitorial_system)___ .
Common law judicatures consequently separate the judiciary from the prosecution,    thereby establishing the courts as completely independent from both the legislature and law enforcement.

Human rights law in these countries is as a result, largely built on legal precedent in the courts' ___E:interpretation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_interpretation)___ of constitutional law, whereas that of civil law countries is almost exclusively composed of codified law, constitutional or otherwise.
There are also international enactments to protect human rights.

One example is the ___E:Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_of_Fundamental_Rights_of_the_European_Union)___ which was intended included in the ___E:Treaty of Lisbon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lisbon)___ .

Perhaps the most important international example is the ___E:Universal Declaration of Human Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Declaration_of_Human_Rights)___ under the ___E:UN Charter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Charter)___ .
These are intended to ensure basic political, social and economic standards that a nation state, or intergovernmental body is obliged to provide to its citizens but many do include its governments.
Another main function of constitutions may be to describe the procedure by which parliaments may legislate.
For instance, special majorities may be required to alter the constitution.
In bicameral legislatures, there may be a process laid out for second or third readings of bills before a new law can enter into force.
Alternatively, there may further be requirements for maximum terms that a government can keep power before holding an ___E:election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election)___ .
Constitutional law is a major focus of legal studies and research.

For example, most law students in the United States are required to take a class in Constitutional Law during their first year, and several ___E:law journals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_journals)___ are devoted to the discussion of constitutional issues.

The doctrine of the ___E:rule of law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law)___ dictates that government must be conducted according to law. This was first established by British legal theorist ___E:A. V. Dicey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._V._Dicey)___ .
Dicey identified three essential elements of the British Constitution which were indicative of the rule of law:
Dicey's rule of law formula consists of three classic tenets.

The first is that the regular law is supreme over arbitrary and discretionary powers. "[N]o man is punishable ... except for a distinct breach of the law established in the ordinary legal manner before the ordinary courts of the land."

The second is that all men are to stand equal in the eyes of the law. "...no man is above the law...every man, whatever be his rank or condition, is subject to the ordinary law of the realm and amenable to the jurisdiction of the ordinary tribunals"

The third is that the general ideas and principles that the constitution supports arise directly from the judgements and precedents issued by the judiciary. "We may say that the constitution is pervaded by the rule of law on the ground that the general principles of the constitution... are with us the result of judicial decisions determining the rights of private persons in particular cases brought before the courts"
___E:Separation of powers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_powers)___ is often regarded as a second limb functioning alongside the rule of law to curb the powers of the government.

In many modern nation states, power is divided and vested into three branches of government: The ___E:legislature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislature)___ , the ___E:executive U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_(government))___ , and the ___E:judiciary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judiciary)___ are known as the horizontal separation of powers.
The first and the second are harmonized in traditional ___E:Westminster system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_system)___ .
Vertical separation of powers is decentralization.
___E:Election law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_law)___ is a subfield of constitutional law. It includes the rules governing the process of elections.
These rules enable the translation of the will of the people into functioning ___E:democracies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy)___ .

Election law addresses issues who is entitled to ___E:vote U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting)___ , ___E:voter registration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voter_registration)___ , ___E:ballot access U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballot_access)___ , ___E:campaign finance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_finance)___ and ___E:party funding U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_party_funding)___ , ___E:redistricting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redistribution_(election))___ , ___E:apportionment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apportionment_(politics))___ , ___E:electronic voting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_voting)___ and ___E:voting machines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_machine)___ , ___E:accessibility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessibility)___ of elections, ___E:election systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_system)___ and formulas, ___E:vote counting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vote_counting)___ , election disputes, ___E:referendums U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum)___ , and issues such as ___E:electoral fraud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud)___ and ___E:electoral silence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_silence)___ .
